## {.act}

::: {.act-kicker}
Act 6 · Explain
:::
::: {.act-question}
Which descriptors does the model use?
:::
::: {.xp data-xp="redline" data-focus="6"}
:::

## Two importances: impurity and permutation {data-station="6"}

![Random forest on all 11 features plus one column of pure random numbers ("noise"). Left: impurity importance. Middle: permutation importance on the training images. Right: permutation importance on a new image (bars: mean of four images; lines: spread).](img/fig_importance.png){width="100%" fig-alt="Three bar charts of feature importance for twelve features; the background feature is important on training data and not on a new image"}

::: {.notes}
- Purpose: two definitions of "important", and why the data that you compute them on matters.
- Impurity importance (MDI, mean decrease in impurity): add the impurity decrease Δ of every split that uses the feature, over all trees. It is free: `rf.feature_importances_`. It is computed from the training data only.
- Permutation importance: take the trained model. Shuffle one column of the test table, so that it has no relation to the labels. Measure how far the score falls. Repeat for each feature. `sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance`.
- Left panel, MDI. The yellow bar is a column of random numbers. It gets 1.2 % of the impurity decrease. Deep trees split on anything in small nodes, also on noise. The bias is stronger for continuous features with many different values.
- The red bar is `bg`, the background under the peak. MDI: 8 %, a middle rank. Middle panel, permutation on the training images: `bg` is the most important feature, 3.6 points. Right panel, permutation on a new image: −0.1 points. Zero.
- So the model uses `bg` strongly, and `bg` does not help on a new image. Both statements are true. Importance on the training images tells you what the model uses. Importance on held-out groups tells you what generalises.
- The same for `amp`: third in the impurity ranking, nearly zero on a new image. On the right, the top places go to `d1`, `d_spread`, `contrast` and `I_rel`.
- Look at the lines on the right panel: the spread between the four images is as large as many bars. Do not rank features that differ by less than this spread.
- Misconception: "feature importance tells me what matters physically." It tells you what this model uses on this data.
- The one point to land: compute permutation importance on held-out groups, and include a noise column as the zero of the scale.
:::

## Correlated descriptors hide each other {data-station="6"}

![Left: permutation importance on a new image for the six invariant descriptors, and again after adding one or two exact copies of d4 to the table. Right: accuracy when the feature is removed and the model is trained again.](img/fig_corr.png){width="96%" fig-alt="Grouped bars of permutation importance with and without copies of one feature, and a bar chart of accuracy after dropping features"}

::: {.claim}
`d4` falls from 11 points to 2.5 to 0 when copies exist. Remove `d1` *or* `d4`: −1 point. Remove both: −6 points.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Purpose: the main trap of permutation importance. This is must-know statement 9.
- The experiment: `d4` is the most important descriptor, 11 points. Add an exact copy of the `d4` column to the table and train again. The importance of `d4` falls to 2.5 points. With two copies it is zero. The information is the same in all three tables.
- Why? The forest spreads its splits over the copies. When you shuffle one copy, the other copies still carry the information, and the score does not fall.
- Real data have no exact copies, but they have correlations. `d1` and `d4` correlate with r = 0.78. Right panel: remove `d1` and train again: 84.1 → 82.9 %. Remove `d4`: 83.2 %. Each one looks nearly useless. Remove both: 77.8 %. Together they carry 6 points.
- A second problem of the shuffle: it makes rows that cannot exist. A column with a nearest-neighbour distance of 0.38 nm and a mean distance of 0.28 nm is not possible; the mean of four distances cannot be below the smallest one. The model has never seen such rows, and its answer there has no meaning. The name is "off-manifold" data.
- The cure: put correlated descriptors into one group, and permute or remove the group together. Find the groups with a correlation matrix or with hierarchical clustering of the features.
- "Drop and retrain" is the honest and expensive version: one new model for each feature group.
- Misconception: "low importance means that I can delete the feature." It can mean that another feature holds the same information.
- The one point to land: importance belongs to groups of correlated features, not to single features.
:::

## SHAP: divide one prediction among the descriptors {data-station="6"}

::: {.deriv}
::: {.dstep .fragment}
[1]{.dnum} **One prediction,** one sum: $f(\mathbf x)=\phi_0+\sum_j\phi_j$
:::
::: {.dstep .fragment}
[2]{.dnum} $\phi_0$ = the mean prediction over the background data.
:::
::: {.dstep .fragment}
[3]{.dnum} $\phi_j$ = the mean change of the prediction when feature $j$ joins, averaged over **all orders** of the features (Shapley value).
:::
::: {.dstep .fragment}
[4]{.dnum} **TreeSHAP:** exact for trees in polynomial time. No sampling.
:::
:::

![Each point: one candidate of image B. Colour: the value of the descriptor.](img/fig_shap.png){width="60%" fig-alt="SHAP summary plot for the class film column with six descriptors; points coloured by descriptor value"}

::: {.notes}
- Purpose: from "which features matter in general" to "why this prediction". Must-know statement 10.
- Step 1: SHAP writes one prediction as a base value plus one signed number for each feature. The sum is exact. The name of this property is completeness, or local accuracy.
- Step 3, the idea from game theory: the features are players, the prediction is the payout. The contribution of a feature depends on which features are already known. So take the mean over all orders. Lundberg and Lee, 2017.
- Step 4: for a general model this needs a sum over 2^F subsets. For trees, an exact algorithm exists that follows the paths of the trees: TreeSHAP, Lundberg and co-workers, 2020. For our forest and 580 columns it takes seconds.
- The figure, the summary plot: one row per descriptor, one point per column of image B. Horizontal position: φ for the class "film column". Right of zero: this descriptor pushes the probability of "film" up for this column. Colour: the value of the descriptor, red is high.
- Read `d_spread`: blue points, a regular neighbourhood, are on the left: −0.13, against "film". This is the substrate. Red points are on the right. Read `d1`: red points, a large nearest distance, are left of zero: the substrate has 0.37 nm. Blue points split into two groups: a moderately small distance supports "film"; a very small distance is on the far left, against "film": these are noise maxima.
- So a SHAP plot also shows non-monotonic relations. `d4` is the clearest: high values appear on both sides.
- Global importance from SHAP: the mean of |φ| for each descriptor. It is a third importance measure, and it has the same problem with correlated features: the credit is divided among them.
- The one point to land: SHAP is an exact accounting of one prediction of the model.
:::

## Click a column: why this prediction? {data-station="6"}

::: {.xp data-xp="shap-click"}
:::

::: {.notes}
- Purpose: read single explanations on the image, and check the sum rule with numbers.
- The image: image B, which the forest did not see in training. The colour of each point is the predicted class. A white ring marks a wrong prediction.
- Demo, step 1: the selected film column near the interface. Read the waterfall from the top. φ₀ = 0.345: the mean predicted probability of "film". `d_spread` = 0.144 adds 0.115. `d1` = 0.289 nm adds 0.107. `d4` = 0.342 nm takes away 0.097. The bars end at 0.655, the prediction. Check line: 0.345 + 0.311 = 0.655.
- Demo, step 2: click a column deep in the substrate. Switch the class to "substrate". All bars point up: a regular square neighbourhood with the right distances.
- Demo, step 3: click a column with a white ring, a wrong prediction, at the border of the amorphous layer. Look for the descriptor that pushed it to the wrong class. Often `psi4` and `d_spread` say "disordered", and the label says "film". The explanation shows that the model and the label disagree about what a film column is.
- Demo, step 4: click one substrate column at the edge of the image. Its neighbours are cut off by the image border, so its descriptors are wrong. The explanation finds a data problem, not a physics result. This is the most common use of SHAP in practice: debugging.
- Ask: "Does a large φ for `d1` mean that the distance causes the class?" No. Next slide.
- The one point to land: an explanation is a tool to find errors in the data, the labels and the descriptors.
:::

## Explanation is not causation {data-station="6"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What SHAP and importance tell you**

- which inputs **this model** uses
- how one prediction divides among the inputs
- where the model uses a nuisance (`bg`, `amp`): a leak detector
- where the labels and the model disagree
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**What they do not tell you**

- what causes the property in the specimen
- what happens if you **change** a descriptor in the experiment
- anything stable under correlated features: the credit is divided
- anything independent of the **background data** that defines $\phi_0$
:::
::::

::: {.claim}
A model can be right for the wrong reason. Only an experiment or a physical model tests a cause.
:::

::: {.notes}
- Purpose: set the limit of everything in this act. The second half of must-know statement 10.
- Left column: these are statements about the model. They are useful. The forest with raw features had a high score on random folds, and its explanation said "background". That finding alone would have told us about the leak, without a second split.
- Right column, point 1 and 2: a descriptor can be a proxy. In our data the thickness of the specimen changes the peak height and also the visibility of the film columns. A model that uses the peak height is not a model of the film.
- Point 3: with correlated descriptors, another forest with another random seed can divide the credit differently between `d1` and `d4`. Report the group.
- Point 4: φ₀ is the mean prediction over a background data set. Change the background, for example from "all images" to "substrate columns only", and every φ changes. Always state the background. For our figure: the training images of the forest, with the path-dependent TreeSHAP.
- Good practice, as a list for the report: (1) the model beats the baseline on grouped folds; (2) permutation importance on held-out groups, with a noise column; (3) correlated features in groups; (4) SHAP for single cases, with the background stated; (5) a check against physics: does the sign make sense?
- The one point to land: explain the model to find its errors. Do not sell the explanation as physics.
- If you are late: skip this slide and say its claim in one sentence.
:::

## Checkpoint: explanations {data-station="6"}

::: {.claim}
Two minutes, in pairs. True or false, and why?
:::

1. "The noise column has an impurity importance of 1 %, so it carries a little information." [→ **False.** MDI is biased; on held-out data it is zero.]{.fragment}
2. "`bg` has the highest permutation importance on the training images, so I must keep it." [→ **False.** On a new image it is zero: it identifies the image.]{.fragment}
3. "`d1` has a low permutation importance, so I can delete it." [→ **Not safe.** `d4` holds the same information. Test the group.]{.fragment}
4. φ₀ = 0.35, the φ sum to +0.31. The predicted probability? [→ **0.66.** Completeness: $f=\phi_0+\sum\phi_j$.]{.fragment}
5. "SHAP shows that a small `d1` causes a film column." [→ **False.** It shows what the model uses. Cause needs an experiment.]{.fragment}

::: {.notes}
- Procedure: two minutes, then reveal.
- Case 1: the noise column is the zero of the scale. Every feature near its value is not distinguishable from noise.
- Case 2: the difference between "used by the model" and "useful for the claim".
- Case 3: remember the right panel of the correlation figure: one removed, 1 point; both removed, 6 points.
- Case 4 is an exam calculation.
- Case 5: the sentence to remember from this act.
- Timing: 3 minutes. If you are late, do cases 2, 3 and 4.
:::

## The red line, complete

::: {.xp data-xp="redline" data-mode="summary"}
:::

::: {.notes}
- Purpose: one picture of the 90 minutes. Each station has its two results.
- Walk along the line. Objects: smooth, find maxima, fit; the dose sets the precision. Descriptors: one row per object, with the invariances built in. Tree: greedy splits on impurity; a deep tree has a high variance. Ensemble: bagging lowers the variance, boosting lowers the bias. Validate: split by image, start with a baseline. Explain: permutation importance on held-out data; SHAP explains the model.
- The arrow back: the score on a new image sent us back to the descriptors, not to a bigger model. From 69 % to 84 % with the same forest.
- The three numbers of the first slide, now with their meaning. 1 934 × 11: the image became a table. 94 % → 69 %: the random split measured the leak. 84 %: invariant descriptors, on an image that the model never saw.
- Connection to Week 4: the same rules, on a new kind of model. Noise model → loss. Complexity → variance. Split → claim.
:::

## Must-know for the exam

::: {.mustknow}
::: {.mk}
[1]{.mk-n} [Classical ML needs a feature table: rows = objects, columns = descriptors. Detection errors propagate into it.]{.mk-t}
:::
::: {.mk}
[2]{.mk-n} [Column finding: smooth → local maxima → 2-D Gaussian fit. Precision ∝ 1/√dose; Poisson likelihood at low dose.]{.mk-t}
:::
::: {.mk}
[3]{.mk-n} [Good descriptors are invariant (translation, rotation, permutation, gain): ratios like $I_\text{rel}$, distances, ACSF/SOAP.]{.mk-t}
:::
::: {.mk}
[4]{.mk-n} [Tree: greedy split with the largest $\Delta = I(\text{parent})-\frac{N_L}{N}I(L)-\frac{N_R}{N}I(R)$. No scaling, no extrapolation, high variance.]{.mk-t}
:::
::: {.mk}
[5]{.mk-n} [Average of $B$ trees: variance $\rho\sigma^2+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$. A random forest lowers $\rho$ with random feature subsets.]{.mk-t}
:::
::: {.mk}
[6]{.mk-n} [Boosting = gradient descent in function space: fit a small tree to $-\partial\mathcal L/\partial F$, add $\eta h$. Early stopping.]{.mk-t}
:::
::: {.mk}
[7]{.mk-n} [Baseline ladder on identical grouped folds: majority → linear → forest/boosting. Good descriptors help the linear model.]{.mk-t}
:::
::: {.mk}
[8]{.mk-n} [Cross-validate by image, session or specimen. Features that identify the image inflate random-split scores.]{.mk-t}
:::
::: {.mk}
[9]{.mk-n} [MDI is biased (noise gets credit). Permutation on held-out groups; permute correlated features together.]{.mk-t}
:::
::: {.mk}
[10]{.mk-n} [SHAP: $f(\mathbf x)=\phi_0+\sum_j\phi_j$, exact for trees. It explains the model, not the cause; it depends on the background.]{.mk-t}
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
- These ten statements are the exam scope of this week. The long version is in the must-know list of the course.
- Each statement has its slide: 1 and 2 in Act 1, 3 in Act 2, 4 in Act 3, 5 and 6 in Act 4, 7 and 8 in Act 5, 9 and 10 in Act 6.
- Typical exam tasks: compute an impurity decrease (checkpoint of Act 3); compute the variance of an ensemble (checkpoint of Act 4); name the group for a validation claim (checkpoint of Act 5); use the SHAP sum rule (checkpoint of Act 6).
:::

## Next week: neural networks & backpropagation

::: {.claim}
Today we designed the descriptors by hand. Next week the model learns its own features, and it must beat today's ladder on the same grouped folds.
:::

- Today: image → **hand-made descriptors** → tree ensemble. 84 % on a new image.
- Next week: a network of simple units learns the descriptors **and** the classifier from the data.
- The tools stay: a loss from the noise model, gradient descent (Week 4), validation by image (today).
- New: the chain rule on a computational graph, **backpropagation**.

::: {.notes}
- Bridge: the weak point of today was the descriptor design. We needed physics knowledge to find `I_rel` and `psi4`, and we still made errors at the image border and at the interface.
- A neural network replaces the hand-made descriptors by learned ones. The price: more data, more compute, and a model that is harder to explain.
- The baseline ladder gets a new rung. The network must beat 84 % on the same leave-one-image-out folds. We will see if it does.
- Preparation: repeat the chain rule and the gradient descent slides of Week 4.
:::

## Backup slides {visibility="uncounted"}

Material outside the 90-minute path, for questions and self-study.

## Gradient boosting in practice {visibility="uncounted"}

| Library | Idea | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| `HistGradientBoosting*` (scikit-learn) | histogram bins, native missing values | default; no extra dependency |
| XGBoost [@chen2016xgboost] | second-order steps, L1/L2 on leaf values | large tables, GPU |
| LightGBM | leaf-wise growth, very fast | very large tables |
| CatBoost [@prokhorenkova2018catboost] | ordered boosting, categorical features | many categorical columns |

**Tuning recipe:** (1) η = 0.05 to 0.1; (2) the number of trees by early stopping on *grouped* validation data; (3) tree size (`max_leaf_nodes` 8 to 64); (4) `min_samples_leaf`, L2; (5) subsampling of rows and columns.

::: {.notes}
- All four libraries implement the algorithm of Act 4. The differences are speed and regularisation.
- The histogram trick: sort each feature once into at most 255 bins. The split search then costs the number of bins, not the number of rows.
- The most common error in practice: early stopping on a random validation split of grouped data. The model stops too late.
:::

## Trees are not rotation invariant {visibility="uncounted"}

![A tree splits along the axes of the table. A boundary that is diagonal in the feature space needs many steps.](img/trees_vs_dl.png){width="80%" fig-alt="Decision boundaries of a tree and of a linear model for an axis-aligned and for a rotated class boundary"}

::: {.notes}
- A tree splits on one feature at a time. A class boundary along a diagonal, for example "d1 − d4 > 0", needs a staircase of many splits.
- For tables this is often an advantage: the columns have a meaning, and physical thresholds apply to single quantities. Grinsztajn and co-workers name this as one reason why trees beat neural networks on tables.
- If you know that a combination matters, for example a ratio or a difference, add it as a descriptor. One good descriptor replaces many splits.
:::

## Out-of-bag error and regression trees {visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Out-of-bag (OOB)**

- a bootstrap sample omits a row with probability $(1-1/N)^N\to e^{-1}\approx 37\,\%$
- predict each row with the trees that did not see it
- a validation score without a second data set
- **grouped data:** OOB rows share the image with training rows → optimistic, like a random split
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Regression trees**

- impurity = variance of $y$ in the node
- a leaf predicts the mean of its rows
- the split minimises the sum of squared errors
- other losses: absolute error (median leaf), Poisson deviance (counts)
- the prediction is piecewise constant: no extrapolation
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
- OOB is useful for a fast check during the development. For the final claim, use the grouped split.
- Regression trees are the weak learners of gradient boosting, also for classification: the trees fit the pseudo-residuals, which are real numbers.
:::

## When the column finder fails {visibility="uncounted"}

| Failure | Sign | Cure |
|---|---|---|
| threshold too low | maxima in the vacuum and in amorphous regions | raise the threshold; classify the candidates (today) |
| σ too large | close columns merge (dumbbells) | smaller σ; fit two Gaussians |
| σ too small | several maxima for one column at low dose | larger σ; a minimum distance |
| image border | cut neighbourhoods, wrong descriptors | discard a margin of one neighbour distance |
| scan distortion, drift | distances change along the slow scan axis | average fast frames; correct the drift first |
| thickness gradient | intensities change across the image | local normalisation (`I_rel`) |

::: {.notes}
- Every row is an error that goes into the feature table, and from there into the model. This is must-know statement 1: detection errors propagate.
- Tools that implement the complete pipeline: Atomap [@nord2017atomap] for atom columns; scikit-image [@vanderwalt2014scikitimage] for segmentation and region properties of particles.
:::

## Checklist: explaining a tabular EM model {visibility="uncounted"}

1. State the claim and the group (image, session, specimen).
2. Report the baseline ladder on identical grouped folds.
3. Add a noise column. Compute permutation importance on held-out groups.
4. Cluster correlated descriptors. Permute or drop the groups.
5. Use SHAP for single cases. State the background data and the model output (probability or log-odds).
6. Check the sign of each main effect against physics.
7. Look at the wrong predictions on the image.
8. Do not claim a cause.

::: {.notes}
- This list is a template for a methods section and for a thesis chapter.
- Points 1 and 2 come from Week 4 and Act 5. Points 3 to 8 are Act 6.
:::
